gap: No result ChatGPT got states Apple's own per-model count for a 13-inch MacBook Air: M1 and M2 drive one external display, M3 drives one with the lid open (a second only with the lid closed), and M4 and M5 drive two with the lid open, so a single-screen extender runs natively on all of them while a two-screen extender shows two extended pictures natively only on M4 and M5.
standout_why: Compared against itechguides.com (cited), lbdsoftware.com (cited) and theofficejournal.com (top result, not cited). itechguides says only that MacBook compatibility "cannot be reduced to 'yes' or 'no'" and depends on the chip generation, with no count per model. lbdsoftware and theofficejournal do not mention a MacBook display limit at all. All three already cover the need for DisplayPort Alt Mode on the USB-C port, charge-only ports, DisplayLink drivers and hinge load, so those parts of the mechanism are not new. techpp.com (cited) returned HTTP 403 and was not read, so it may already carry the counts. ChatGPT's own answer gestures at "different external-display limits" without numbers, which is why this is 2 and not 3.
decides: It confirms a single added screen as the pick for a 13-inch laptop. Apple lists one external display and native DisplayPort over USB-C for the M2 Air, and at least one for the M3, M4 and M5 Air, so a one-screen extender on USB-C needs no driver on those 13-inch MacBook Airs. Plugable gives the same one-display figure for M1. It also draws the line for the two-screen rows (FOPO S1, FOPO S7): on an M1, M2 or lid-open M3 Air the second added screen cannot be a native extended display, and Apple says daisy-chaining does not raise the maximum. Those rows should be labelled for M4 and M5 Airs or Windows laptops with two video-capable ports, or need a DisplayLink-type driver path. For the page's two required linked rows, the Duex Plus DS 13.3-inch is sold by our partner Mobile Pixels at $183.99 today but has no record yet. I could not source a maker-stated 13-inch fit range for it or for the FOPO S1 and S7 (store pages rate-limited); if neither FOPO row states 13 inches, the page falls short of two rows.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (M2, 2022), Apple's figure
findings.value: 1 external display, up to 6K at 60 Hz, alongside the built-in display; "Native DisplayPort output over USB-C"
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (M2, 2022) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's Display Support section. Two Thunderbolt / USB 4 ports, both listed with DisplayPort support, so either port can carry the one added screen without a driver.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air (13-inch, M3, 2024), Apple's figure
findings.value: 1 external display up to 6K at 60 Hz with the lid open; a second, up to 5K at 60 Hz, only with the lid closed
findings.source_title: MacBook Air (13-inch, M3, 2024) - Tech Specs - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's words: "Close the MacBook Air lid to use a second external display with up to 5K resolution at 60Hz". An extender mounted behind the lid needs the lid open, so the usable count there is one.

findings.label: External displays, MacBook Air with M4 or M5, Apple's figure
findings.value: Up to 2 external displays in addition to the built-in display; closing the lid does not raise the count
findings.source_title: How many displays can be connected to MacBook Air - Apple Support
findings.note: Page dated March 10, 2026. Two displays up to 6K at 60 Hz or 4K at 144 Hz. Apple adds that daisy-chaining can put two displays on one Thunderbolt port "but does not increase the maximum".

findings.label: External displays, base M1 and M2 Macs, and how a driver screen gets past the limit (Plugable)
findings.value: M1/M2: 1 external display via Thunderbolt, up to 6K at 60 Hz. DisplayLink "combines software and hardware to send video signals over USB data connections", which allows displays beyond the native count
findings.source_title: Understanding External Display Support on Apple M1, M2, M3, M4 and M5 Chips - Plugable Knowledge Base
findings.note: Last updated August 28, 2026. Plugable sells DisplayLink docks, so this is a vendor's explanation. It also states that natively extended displays "cannot exceed what is natively supported by the Thunderbolt ports". This is my only opened source for the M1 figure; I did not open Apple's M1 spec page.
